Replace dictionary terms, in parallel

Source: R/par-match-term.R
par_replace_term.Rd

Replaces every term of terms in each string with its replacement, such as to normalize spellings, expand abbreviations, or redact names. It does what a gsub(fixed = TRUE) per term would, but in one pass, however many terms there are.

Usage

par_replace_term(
  x,
  terms,
  replacement,
  ignore_case = FALSE,
  whole_word = FALSE,
  fixed = TRUE,
  nthreads = getOption("parvenu.threads", 0L)
)

Arguments

x

A string vector, or an object convertible by as.character().

terms

A string vector of literal strings to find. NA is not allowed, nor "" unless fixed = FALSE.

replacement

A string vector as long as terms, the replacement for each, or one string for all of them. With fixed = FALSE, $1 stands for the first capture group of the term's match, as in par_replace_all().

ignore_case

If TRUE, letters match regardless of case, in any script: "é" matches "É". ASCII letters cost nothing extra. Strings with other characters are lowercased first. With fixed = FALSE, this is (?i).

whole_word

If TRUE, a term counts only where it isn't part of a longer word. "york" then matches "new york" and "york, uk", but not "yorkshire". The characters right before and after the term must not be word characters, those \\w matches. These are letters, digits, and marks (such as an accent written as a character of its own) in any script, and _. An apostrophe (' or the curly \u2019) between two word characters joins them into one word. So "won" doesn't match "won't", nor "heaven" "heaven's". With fixed = FALSE, the same goes for a term's match.

If "start", a term must start a word but may end inside one, as a prefix: "happ" matches "happy" and "happiness", but not "unhappy". This is the "happ*" of dictionaries such as LIWC.

fixed

If FALSE, terms are regexes, in the syntax of par_detect().

nthreads

A whole number: the max number of threads to use. 0 means the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable, or else all cores. The default is the parvenu.threads option, or 0 if that isn't set. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy get fewer, and more threads than cores count as all cores.

Value

A string vector as long as x, NA where x is NA. It keeps the names of x, as gsub() does.

Details

Since it is one pass, a replacement is never searched again for the terms after it.

Hits don't overlap. The leftmost hit is replaced first, and the search goes on after it. If several terms start at the same place, the one earliest in terms wins. So put longer terms before their prefixes, such as "new york" before "new". A regex term that can match the empty string, such as "x*", has an empty hit at each place without another hit, but not right where a longer hit ended, as in par_replace_all().

Examples

par_replace_term(
  c("NYC and LA", "la la land"),
  c("NYC", "LA"),
  c("New York City", "Los Angeles"),
  whole_word = TRUE
)
#> [1] "New York City and Los Angeles" "la la land"                   

# Redaction
par_replace_term("Ann met Bob", c("ann", "bob"), "[name]", ignore_case = TRUE)
#> [1] "[name] met [name]"

# Longer terms first
par_replace_term("new york, new jersey", c("new york", "new"), c("NY", "N."))
#> [1] "NY, N. jersey"
